items.title: The AI Regulation Puzzle: Regulatory Capture, Capital Factionalism, and the Big Pharma Parallel
items.abstract: This paper argues that the artificial intelligence industry is following the Big Pharma playbook of regulatory influence—but with a critical difference. Unlike the pharmaceutical industry, which presents a unified front against binding regulation, the AI industry is fractured into twoopenly warring factions: an "Accelerationist" bloc led by OpenAI and Andreessen Horowitz,which opposes binding regulation; and a "Safety" bloc led by Anthropic, which advocates for stricter guardrails. This internal fracture complicates the regulatory capture thesis. However,a third actor—the military-industrial complex, represented by the Pentagon—has resolvedthe debate in the military domain through coercive power rather than regulatory capture. Through supply-chain designations, contract coercion, and judicial victories, the Pentagonhas effectively mandated that AI companies surrender their ethical constraints for militaryuse. This paper integrates the Pentagon's position into the analysis, arguing that the AIindustry's political economy is now structured by three dynamics: the MIC's coercive authority over military AI, capital factionalism over civilian regulation, and the structural absence of Congress from both domains. The Big Pharma parallel illuminates themechanisms of influence but fails to capture the full picture: in military AI, there is noregulation to capture because the state has imposed its preferences directly throughprocurement power. Keywords: military-industrial complex, AI governance, regulatory capture, supply chain risk, autonomous weapons, Pentagon

items.title: The AI Risk Economy
items.abstract: Economic incentives drive how organizations deploy AI. Companies push ahead faster and accept more risk to capture profit, a structural tendency the author calls the Economic Override Pattern, and countering it requires economic pressure that makes bypassing governance cost more than complying with it. This paper examines liability and insurance as that counter-pressure: liability attaches the cost of AI failure to the business, and insurance can turn that cost into coverage terms at every renewal, so that proving a human stays in control becomes a financial advantage. The commercial insurance industry is responding to artificial intelligence risk through exclusion endorsements, conditional coverage, and standalone AI liability products. The paper asks whether that response is beginning to sort AI deployments by governance maturity, and it proposes a five-tier insurance maturity model mapping organizational AI governance posture to insurability. Carriers exclude AI risk because they have no tables to assess it. The five-tier model proposes how the market should assess that risk in tiers, in the traditional form, until longitudinal loss data exists. The model distinguishes between organizations with no AI policy, published ethical principles, automated technical controls, named human checkpoint authority, and structured audit records. The evidence suggests the market is beginning to sort AI deployments by governance evidence at its specialty edge, through access to affirmative coverage, while standard-market exclusions and silent coverage remain largely blind to governance maturity. Validated premium differentials have not yet emerged. The paper documents AI exclusion forms or filings from several named carriers and from Verisk, with primary form text confirmed for three carriers and for two of Verisk's three ISO endorsements. The earliest of those forms bears a mid-2023 revision date. Trade analysis reported that 41 property and casualty insurance groups had at least one subsidiary file to adopt an AI exclusion by July 2026, though a filing to adopt is not proof of use. It also notes a reported Verisk study of exclusions aimed at agentic AI. Affirmative coverage now comes from nine providers offering ten distinct products. Twenty-five U.S. states plus the District of Columbia had adopted the NAIC AI Model Bulletin as of August 31, 2026. The evidence base was assembled through a parallel multi-AI research methodology using 12 AI platforms dispatched independently, with hallucination detection, then updated through live source verification and a cross-platform check in September 2026. The paper's central empirical finding is the missing link in that mechanism, an actuarial gap. Theoretical frameworks published through September 2026 place governance maturity inside AI insurance pricing models, but no published empirical study was located that quantifies governance maturity as a pricing factor for AI liability insurance. The paper also argues that the insurance thesis holds whether negligence, strict liability, or regulatory enforcement governs a claim. It then asks whether AI policies that prohibit assistive use create exposure of their own. The frameworks proposed here represent the author's professional judgment applied to observed market signals, offered as a starting point for a field that does not yet have one.

items.title: The Epistemics of Agent Memory: Measuring, and Governing, the Consolidation Decision in Long-Horizon LLM Agents
items.abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents must convert accumulated experience into durable memory, deciding what to keep, compress, abstract into reusable skills and rules, or forget. We report a four-phase research program on this consolidation problem whose central finding is a shift in what is measured: from how much an agent remembers, to whether its consolidation decisions are any good, to whether those decisions can be trusted. Phase 1 learns episodic boundaries from agent traces by downstream utility; an honest near-miss (oracle correlation 0.691 vs a 0.70 bar) whose lasting output is a three-gate anti-leakage protocol. Phase 2 learns when to promote experience and to which abstraction level under a token budget, achieving a verified +22.7% task-success improvement with 7x compression, but exposing a degenerate-forgetting failure and a distribution-shift failure mode we name lambda-prevalence coupling. Phase 3 introduces ConsolidationBench, an oracle-by-construction benchmark that scores consolidation decisions against a known optimum on three non-circular axes; production retrieval systems retain information yet score zero on cross-level transfer. Phase 4 introduces governed consolidation: the decision wrapped in poison-resistance, reversibility, and auditability guarantees with a quality gate. Governance is statistically distinct from the quality score ($r^2 = 0.43$; partial $r = 0.27$; identical-quality policies differ threefold in governance), so the contribution survives independently of the metric's external validity. On that question we report a resolved negative: after a graded-reuse redesign removed a structural ceiling, a two-benchmark study with 2,532 real answer cells finds the quality score does not predict real transfer accuracy (pooled Spearman $ρ= -0.24$, n = 12, CI spanning zero). An adversarial self-critique pass cleared the final claim set with zero surviving overclaims.

items.title: The Legal Framework for Governing Artificial Intelligence in Iraqi Commercial Companies: A Critical Analysis of Legislative Challenges and A Regulatory Model
items.abstract: Purpose: This study examines the adequacy of the existing Iraqi legal framework for regulating the growing use of artificial intelligence in commercial companies. It focuses on emerging legal challenges related to liability, privacy, algorithmic discrimination, employee rights, and consumer protection. Design/Methodology/Approach: The study adopts a qualitative, analytical-critical, and comparative legal research design. It analyses Iraqi legislation and official materials and compares them with selected international and regional AI governance frameworks, using risk, accountability, rights, oversight, and enforcement as the principal analytical dimensions. The IR-CAGM is developed as the normative output of this analysis. Research Limitation: The study focuses primarily on the Iraqi legal framework and comparative regulatory models and does not empirically assess the implementation of artificial intelligence regulations within individual companies. Findings: Existing Iraqi laws can address certain legal implications of artificial intelligence; however, these provisions remain fragmented, largely interpretative, and reactive. Major legislative gaps include the absence of a clear legal definition of artificial intelligence, risk-based classification, clear allocation of liability between companies and suppliers, comprehensive data protection legislation, and effective rights to explanation and objection. The comparative analysis further indicates that directly transferring foreign regulatory models would not adequately reflect the Iraqi legal and institutional context. Practical Implication: The proposed IR-CAGM model provides a phased framework connecting legislation, sectoral oversight, corporate responsibility, impact assessment, life-cycle governance, and individual rights. Social Implication: The model can strengthen public trust, protect fundamental rights, and support responsible technological innovation. Originality/Value: The study proposes a hybrid, context-sensitive regulatory model that balances artificial intelligence innovation, corporate accountability, and rights protection in Iraq.

items.title: The Most Important Human Skills for the Age of AI and the Future of Work: FILE — The Five Intelligences of Leadership Evolution
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence changes what organizations can do; human leadership must decide what should be done, what remains accountable, and what must never be surrendered to machines. This working paper presents FILE: The Five Intelligences of Leadership Evolution as a human-centered management theory and diagnostic framework for responsible leadership and decision-making in the age of artificial intelligence and robotics. FILE argues that the most important human skills for the AI era and the future of work require the integrated exercise of five meta-intelligences: Augmented Intelligence, Emotional Intelligence, Cultural Intelligence, Political Intelligence, and Adaptive Intelligence. The paper defines the FILE formula, maps the framework onto the human hand, presents the 70 foundational nested intelligences, the 128-intelligence Teaching and Diagnostic Framework, and the 163-intelligence Extended Taxonomy, explains five emergent outcomes, and develops RC: The Relational Commons as the shared human ecosystem that leadership must protect, cultivate, and renew. It also clarifies boundaries among adjacent intelligences, offers a diagnostic application to AI-supported employee performance evaluation, and states limitations and future research directions. Its purpose is to establish a public, citable, and timestamped record of FILE as a transdisciplinary theory of human leadership in the age of AI and robots.

items.title: The Newly Discovered Leishmaniasis Vaccine is a Live Prepared Vaccine Made by In-Silico AI
items.abstract: ABSTRACT- About Leishmaniasis is a disease caused by a protozoan parasite Leishmania donovani complex. Leishmaniasis is one of the major diseases which is a major neglected tropical diseases that lack the licensed human vaccine and prevalent in Bihar, Jharkhand, West Bengal, and 98 other countries. The present invention also describes a novel live-attenuated vaccine candidate prepared in combined in-vivo animal model done by in-Silico AI, in-vitro culture done by In-Silico AI and in-silico Artificial Intelligence optimization by softwares. In this study,by using Insilico AI live promastigote of L. donovani (Strain AG83) was attenuated by serial in-vivo passages in BALB/c mice, golden hamster and in-vitro cultivation in NNN medium with genetic attenuation of centrin and p27 gene. The live leishmania parasite was immunogenic but non-virulent. In order to optimize the vaccine as safe and efficacious, in-silico AI tools such as Alpha Fold2, IEDB epitope prediction, molecular docking and immune simulation was used to find the most conserved immunodominant epitopes from antigenic proteins such as gp63, LACK, KMP-11 and amastigote specific A2 proteins. AI prediction revealed stable multi-epitope chimeras with high MHC-I /MHC-II binding affinities and TLR-4 adjuvant activity.

items.title: The Record Can Be Rewritten, the Consequences Remain: Archives, Artificial Intelligence, and the Memory of War
items.abstract: The long-term consequences of war exist independently of how archives, registers, and publications record them. Yet information systems often treat the surviving record as reality. The absence of a document is confused with the absence of an event, while an archival classification becomes a description of a person, victim, or process. This paper treats the archive as a historically formed and adjusted distorted mirror. The state sets a political direction, while the expert community translates it into categories, catalogues, and authoritative knowledge. Rewriting the past must therefore be understood as a long-term consequence of war. Data on victims, mass graves, and conflicting evidence require four levels: what happened, surviving evidence, human and institutional interpretations, and algorithmic conclusions. Artificial intelligence reduces the cost of comparing bodies of documents and allows small groups to test official versions of the past. It can automate political distortions and give unproven conclusions the appearance of knowledge. A reliable information system must preserve the origin of every claim, contradictions, uncertainty, and the history of corrections. Its task is not to create a final past, but to prevent interpretations from destroying evidence and presenting themselves as reality.

items.title: The Role of MOOCs-Based Learning Environment Support in Enhancing Self-Regulated Learning: Evidence from Hope School, Southwest Jiaotong University
items.abstract: The objectives of this research were 1. to identify the functional shortcomings of the current MOOC platform 2. to empirically examine how platform usability, resource richness and interactivity, together with learners’ intrinsic motivation, autonomy and self-efficacy, jointly influence graduate students’ sustained adoption of MOOCs and 3. to propose and validate a dual strategy of system optimization and individual empowerment including streamlined system functions, enriched learning resources, strengthened teacher–student interaction and personalized support that enhance postgraduates' MOOC usage willingness and autonomous learning ability. A quantitative research design was employed, with data collected from postgraduate students at Hope School, Southwest Jiaotong University. The data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) a total of 703 sample data were collected. The research results indicate that 1) high-quality learning environment support particularly in terms of system quality and ease of use has a significant positive effect on expectation confirmation and learner satisfaction. These factors serve as critical mediators in the development of self-regulated learning skills, most notably in goal setting, progress monitoring, and self-reflection. 2) The results underscore the necessity of adopting an integrated strategy that combines the enhancement of learning technology systems with the empowerment of learners’ self-regulatory capacities in order to promote effective and sustainable online learning in postgraduate education and 3) MOOC-platform learning-environment support, learners’ self-efficacy and self-regulated learning ability are the key drivers of perceived usefulness and satisfaction. Expectation confirmation influences perceived usefulness.

items.title: The Synthetic Labour Tipping Point
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is changing more than the productivity of individual workers. It is changing who or what can perform organizational work.AI systems can increasingly interpret information, solve specified problems, coordinate activities and initiate actions within defined parameters. As these capabilities become embedded in organizations, automation of individual activities alone stops being the core issue. The economic question is whether an organization is better off having a synthetic entity perform a particular activity. The larger issue is what happens when enough activities shift in that direction to reshape the organization around them.Synthetic Labour Tipping Point. This paper develops the concept of the Synthetic Labour Tipping Point: the point at which synthetic execution becomes extensive enough to alter the economics and organization of the work surrounding it. Individual activities will cross this threshold at different times. The organizational question arises when changes across interdependent activities begin to affect coordination, supervision, decision-making and structure.The paper distinguishes synthetic execution from synthetic agency. Synthetic execution concerns performance: who or what actually does the work. Synthetic agency concerns authority: who or what is assigned the decision rights. items.title: Toward intelligent safety assurance in construction human-robot collaboration
items.abstract: Construction human-robot collaboration (HRC) introduces physical, ergonomic, and cognitive risks that conventional isolated-based safeguards cannot adequately manage in dynamic, unstructured worksites and requires more adaptive forms of safety assurance. Although diverse robotics-related approaches have been developed, how they function as interconnected, active safety-assurance mechanisms for construction HRC remains insufficiently synthesised. This paper systematically reviews 215 studies published from 2011 to 2025 through PRISMA-guided screening, bibliometric analysis and thematic synthesis. Five connected technological directions are identified: robot design optimisation, context-aware perception, human-centric understanding and forecasting, autonomous robotic adaptation, and safety management. The synthesis shows a transition from passive risk avoidance toward perception-driven, prediction, and adaptive safety assurance, but 54% of studies remain limited to controlled laboratory validation, and few integrate uncertainty across sensing, prediction, control and supervision. Accordingly, a closed-loop framework is proposed to guide the integration and construction-realistic validation of verifiable, uncertainty-aware HRC safety systems.

items.title: Towards Capability Development: A Layered Analysis of AIS Replay and Ghost Ship Attacks
items.abstract: The Automatic Identification System (AIS) is a fundamental component of modern Maritime Situational Awareness (MSA) systems, supporting navigation safety, vessel traffic management, and maritime surveillance. However, the absence of authentication, integrity protection, and message verification makes AIS vulnerable to a range of spoofing attacks capable of manipulating the maritime operational picture. Although existing research has proposed various techniques for detecting AIS spoofing, comparatively little attention has been given to understanding how different spoofing mechanisms influence operational behaviour and the capabilities required to detect and respond to them. To address this gap, the paper introduces a focused taxonomy that distinguishes replay and ghost ship attacks, while accounting for hybrid scenarios that combine characteristics of both mechanisms. A layered threat analysis characterises their observable manifestations across the physical, network infrastructure, AIS protocol, AIS message validation, and operational behaviour layers and identifies the distinct operational capabilities required to detect, distinguish, and respond to these attacks. Building upon this analysis, the paper proposes a structured capability-driven cyber range exercise design approach that systematically translates these capabilities into learning objectives and differentiated training scenarios. Furthermore, the work contributes guidelines for evaluating participants’ performance in alignment with the proposed operational capabilities and learning objectives. Overall, the work provides a structured analytical framework for understanding AIS replay and ghost ship attacks, and their combination, and a practical approach for developing capability-driven maritime cybersecurity training aligned with their operational characteristics.

items.title: Transformasi Hukum Berkeadilan di Era Digital: Peluang dan Tantangannya di Indonesia
items.abstract: Digital transformation has brought significant changes to various aspects of human life, including the legal system. Advances in information and communication technology have stimulated the emergence of various digital-based legal innovations, such as electronic court services, digital signatures, artificial intelligence in law enforcement, and regulations governing electronic transactions. This study aims to analyze the transformation of justice-oriented law in the digital era by examining the opportunities and challenges arising from its implementation. The research employs a normative legal research method using both the statutory and conceptual approaches. The findings indicate that legal digitalization offers substantial opportunities to enhance the effectiveness, efficiency, transparency, and public access to justice. On the other hand, this transformation also presents several challenges, including the digital divide, personal data protection, cybersecurity, the potential misuse of technology, and the inadequacy of existing legal regulations to keep pace with rapid technological developments. Therefore, adaptive, responsive, and justice-oriented legal reform is essential to ensure that legal transformation in the digital era is not solely focused on technological advancement but also guarantees the protection of human rights and legal certainty for all members of society.

items.title: Transforming Pharmacovigilance Through Artificial Intelligence: Current Trends and Future Perspectives
items.abstract: Pharmacovigilance plays a crucial role in detecting, assessing, understanding, and preventing adverse drug reactions throughout the life cycle of medicines. However, the increasing volume, complexity, and diversity of safety data have created significant limitations for conventional, mainly manual and reactive pharmacovigilance systems. Artificial intelligence (AI) provides an opportunity to transform pharmacovigilance into a more efficient, continuous, predictive, and patient-centric system. This review explores the current applications, emerging technologies, challenges, and future perspectives of AI-driven pharmacovigilance. Machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, data mining, knowledge graphs, robotic process automation, computer vision, large language models, and generative AI can support several pharmacovigilance activities, including individual case safety report processing, case coding and classification, duplicate detection, adverse drug reaction identification, signal detection, causality assessment, predictive risk assessment, and risk–benefit evaluation. AI can reduce repetitive workload, improve processing efficiency, identify patterns within large and unstructured datasets, and support earlier detection of potential safety signals. Emerging approaches such as explainable AI, multimodal AI, federated learning, digital twins, and human–AI collaboration may further improve transparency, privacy, prediction, and individualized safety monitoring. Nevertheless, challenges related to data quality, heterogeneity, algorithmic bias, interoperability, validation, explainability, privacy, cybersecurity, infrastructure, cost, and regulatory requirements remain important barriers. Successful implementation therefore requires robust data infrastructure, validated and interpretable models, appropriate governance, regulatory alignment, continuous monitoring, and skilled pharmacovigilance professionals. Overall, AI is expected to augment rather than replace human expertise and may enable earlier, more personalized, and proactive drug safety decision-making.

items.title: TRENDS IN STUDENT PERCEPTIONS OF CHATGPT: EVIDENCE FROM A THREE-YEAR GLOBAL STUDY
items.abstract: This study examines global student perceptions of ChatGPT in higher education across three academic years. Drawing on survey data from 66,923 students worldwide, it analyzes changes in usage patterns, satisfaction, and attitudes. The findings reveal substantial growth in ChatGPT use across all analyzed tasks, particularly for study assistance and summarizing. Students generally perceived ChatGPT as useful, supportive, and increasingly valuable for academic work. At the same time, declining novelty and reduced perceived control indicate a shift from initial enthusiasm toward normalization, suggesting that ChatGPT is becoming embedded in students’ everyday academic practices.

items.title: Trust and Task Completion in the World of Consumer AI Agents
items.abstract: Action agents do things for people. They send email, spend money, and call businesses while the user is busy with something else, so a mistake can turn into an action before anyone notices. They fail their users in two ways. They break trust when they do something the user never agreed to, or hold back after the user clearly said go. And they fall short on completion when they give up on errands that turn out to be hard. Both depend heavily on the harness around the model, meaning its instructions, tools, context, and guardrails. We built an evaluation that scores trust and completion on the same runs, in a simulated world of businesses with their own websites, inboxes, and phone lines, and of people who write back. A simulated user answers the assistant's questions. Trust means that nothing happens the user did not agree to. No email goes to someone they never approved, no private detail ends up on a group thread, no money is spent past their limit, no stranger's instructions are followed, and nothing is claimed without a source. Every trap has a matched control in which acting is the right call. We use the evaluation to measure Fo, Wajo's personal assistant, against a base model with basic instructions on three foundation models, and against the Fo harness with its guardrails switched off. Fo completes 71% of the errands and keeps the user's trust on 94% of the trap runs. The base models complete 50% to 64% and keep trust on 59% to 75%. On the matched controls, Fo goes ahead slightly less often. OpenClaw, a popular open-source assistant given the same access, completes 42% of the errands it shares with Fo, against 71%, and keeps the user's trust on 74% of the shared trap runs, against 94%. Measuring trust and completion together, on the whole system rather than the model alone, is how we think action agents become safe to hand real work to.

items.title: Trust the Brand, Lose Control: How Identity Hijacks LLM Agent Orchestration
items.abstract: LLM agents now execute tasks end to end with permission to change real systems and increasingly orchestrate subagents that differ in capability and cost. Prior work treats the choice of subagent as an optimization problem. Yet the orchestrator makes this choice from the identities that subagents display, and an attacker can spoof them. Displayed identity thus decides operational authority, meaning who is trusted to check the work and who is allowed to change it. As a result, a risky subagent can keep authority over execution even after other evidence contradicts it. We introduce TrustFork, an LLM agent safety benchmark with 1,890 tasks and 27,826 valid trajectories across 16 agent systems. These systems run eight orchestrators under the OpenCode, OpenClaw, and Pi harnesses. In each task, one subagent carries a risky goal while the other three stay aligned with the user, so contradicting evidence can exist. A task can also change the identity a subagent displays without changing the model behind it, which lets us trace a shift in authority to the label. Our analysis shows that even when another subagent contradicts the risky response, the orchestrator still acts on it in 72.0% of cases on average, most often in the systems with the least terminal harm. Swapping the family labels nearly triples how often the orchestrator obtains the risky response. A safer response is available in 84.0% of tasks, yet it decides the outcome in only 25.0%. The harness also decides which responses reach the orchestrator. Among three runtime defenses, hiding identity cues helps most consistently, while verifying before action helps only when the harness returns enough evidence. TrustFork shows that production agent orchestration must bind authority to evidence before execution causes harm. Our project is in https://henrymao2004.github.io/agent-orchestration-safety/.

items.title: Understanding and Exploiting Anisotropy in Post-Training
items.abstract: LLM post-training combines supervised fine-tuning (SFT), a mode-covering forward-KL objective, with reinforcement learning (RL), a mode-seeking reverse-KL objective. Frequency-weighted likelihood training leaves a well-known signature: \emph{anisotropy}, in which a few residual channels carry disproportionately large activations. Anisotropy is widely documented and usually treated as a defect, yet its function and its interaction with post-training remain unclear. We first analyze it. A label-free outlier rule isolates about 5\% of residual channels that are essential for language modeling: removing them raises perplexity from 10 to over $10^6$, versus 35 for count-matched random channels. Yet they barely distinguish correct from incorrect reasoning. SFT reshapes them, whereas RL leaves them largely intact and adapts the complementary channels. These channels therefore form the model's \emph{coherence substrate}, and reasoning adaptation happens elsewhere. We then exploit this. \textsc{SphereGate} learns one bounded gain per residual channel on a frozen backbone. Its activation-weighted gradients provably limit movement of high-energy coherence channels and leave the remaining channels free. With 0.1M trainable parameters, \textsc{SphereGate} outperforms parameter-efficient baselines by 2.0--7.3 points on MATH-500 across Qwen2.5 (0.5B--7B) and Llama-3-8B, is comparable or exceeds full-model GRPO. Anisotropy is not a defect but a division of labor that post-training can exploit.

items.title: Unit fractions with semiprime denominators: an elementary proof of Erdős Problem #306
items.abstract: We give an elementary proof that every positive rational number $a/b$ with $b$ squarefree is a finite sum of distinct unit fractions $1/n$, where each $n$ is a product of two distinct primes (Erdős Problem #306). After a reduction to small targets, we take a single complete bipartite graph between the primes in $(y^2,2y^2]$, together with $2$ and the primes of $b$, and a tuned initial segment of the primes in $(y^8,y^9]$, and show that some subgraph has reciprocal sum congruent to $a/b$ modulo $1$; the small total mass then forces equality. Writing the number of such subgraphs as a finite Fourier sum, we sort the frequencies into three cases using a table indexed by the two sides of the graph. The small integer frequencies give a positive main term, and all other frequencies are negligible by a divisor-counting argument and a no-wrap-around form of the Chinese remainder theorem. The only inputs about primes are Chebyshev-type bounds. The circle-method framework comes from Tang's Lean development, which gave the first proof; our construction removes its anchor-synchronisation step. The proof has been formalised in Lean 4, apart from a cited inequality of Ramanujan. This work is a human-AI collaboration: AI tools contributed substantially to the construction, the experiments and the writing.

items.title: User Experience and Satisfaction With a Web‐Based Application to Improve Intelligibility in Parkinson's Disease
items.abstract: BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: Motor speech impairments, such as hypokinetic dysarthria, are highly prevalent among individuals with Parkinson's disease (PD). These voice and speech deficits may significantly impact speech intelligibility, leading many individuals with PD to withdraw socially. Digital platforms may provide a feasible way to address motor speech impairments in this population while also fostering patients' self-management skills through independent home-based practice. The objective of this preliminary one-group pre-post treatment study is to provide a qualitative examination of participants' experience and satisfaction using a custom-developed web-based application to improve speech intelligibility using noise-augmented automatic speech recognition feedback. METHODS: Four individuals with PD completed one month (= 16 sessions) of a novel intensive speech treatment program through a web-based application with weekly online support from a speech-language pathologist. At post-treatment, participants completed individual interviews to document their user experience with the digital platform and a brief satisfaction survey. Interviews were analysed qualitatively following an experiential orientation and reflexive thematic analysis. RESULTS: Overall, participants were satisfied with their experience using the app. Four themes were generated from the data set: (1) From external feedback to metacognitive awareness, (2) two worlds colliding, (3) beyond voice and speech gains: Psychosocial benefits of noise-augmented automatic speech recognition, and (4) reconciling the demands of a digital interface with the motor and non-motor symptoms of Parkinson's disease. CONCLUSIONS: Qualitative data yields preliminary support for the use of a digital speech web-based application that provides noise-augmented automatic speech recognition feedback to improve intelligibility in individuals with PD. Results support further testing of this protocol with a larger cohort of participants in a controlled environment. WHAT THIS PAPER ADDS: What is already known on this subject Motor speech impairments, such as hypokinetic dysarthria, are highly prevalent among individuals with Parkinson's disease (PD). These voice and speech deficits may significantly impact speech intelligibility, leading many individuals with PD to withdraw socially. Digital platforms may provide a feasible way to address motor speech impairments in this population while also fostering patients' self-management skills through independent home-based practice. Digital tools for speech rehabilitation in this population are emerging in the field. However, no digital tool has explored the role of automatic speech recognition (ASR) in noise as a treatment method. Hence, user experience for this novel and naturalistic method warrants further investigation. What this study adds to the existing knowledge The objective of this one-group pre-post treatment study is to provide a qualitative examination of participants' experience and satisfaction using a custom-developed web-based application to improve speech intelligibility using noise-augmented ASR feedback. To the authors' knowledge, this is the first study to describe this novel approach, powered by artificial intelligence, and provide a qualitative examination of this naturalistic method targeting intelligibility. This information will guide future iterations of this web-based technology and provide preliminary insights into how noise-augmented ASR feedback can contribute to patient management. What are the clinical implications of this study? Patient-led digital technologies leveraging ASR in noise hold promise for clinical practice. For the participants with dysarthria secondary to PD in our study, a novel speech treatment that targets intelligibility through noise-augmented ASR feedback was deemed useful and promising to improve not only their voice and speech but also to increase their awareness of how dysarthria impacts their voice in noisy conditions. Additionally, some participants reported increases in confidence and motivation to communicate, which underscores a promising psychosocial impact of this approach.

items.title: Using Artificial Intelligence Systems to Improve the Performance and Sustainability of Production Processes in The Iraqi Oil and Gas Sector
items.abstract: Purpose: The purpose of this study is to analyse the relationship between artificial intelligence (AI) applications and the achievement of sustainability in the Iraqi oil and gas sector by exploring the available opportunities and potential risks associated with adopting intelligent technologies and proposing a roadmap for their effective utilisation. Design/Methodology/Approach: The study adopts a descriptive analytical approach supported by an applied exploratory method. AI is considered the independent variable and is measured through five dimensions: predictive and intelligent analytics systems, predictive maintenance, robotics and autonomous systems, big data analytics, and intelligent decision support systems. Sustainability is the dependent variable and is measured through its environmental, economic, and social dimensions. The study was conducted in 2025 within the Iraqi oil and gas sector, particularly companies operating in Basra Governorate. A total of 165 questionnaires were distributed, of which 151 valid responses were received, representing a response rate of 91.5%. The data were analysed using SPSS through reliability and validity tests and multiple regression analysis. Research Limitation: The study is limited to the Iraqi oil and gas sector, particularly companies operating in Basra Governorate, and the data were collected during 2025. The findings are based on questionnaire responses and may therefore have limited generalizability to other sectors or geographical contexts. Findings: The results indicate a statistically significant relationship between the application of AI technologies and the achievement of sustainability. The findings confirm that AI technologies contribute to improving operational performance while enhancing environmental, economic, and social sustainability within the Iraqi oil and gas sector. Practical Implication: The study recommends establishing an integrated system to periodically and systematically measure the impact of AI technologies on sustainability, enabling organisations to improve operational efficiency and support sustainable development objectives. Social Implication: The adoption of AI technologies can enhance environmental protection, improve workplace safety, and promote sustainable practices that contribute to broader social and economic development within the Iraqi oil and gas sector. Originality/Value: The study contributes to the limited body of research on AI adoption and sustainability in the Iraqi oil and gas sector by examining AI through five technological dimensions and sustainability through its environmental, economic, and social dimensions, providing empirical evidence and a practical roadmap for the effective implementation of AI to support sustainability.

items.title: Virginia Tech: Comprehensive AI Governance & Activity Inventory
items.abstract: A public-source inventory of artificial intelligence governance, teaching, research, and operations at Virginia Tech. Evidence snapshot date: September 26, 2026. The document records what the university has said and done publicly about AI as of that date. It is not an audit, maturity assessment, or scorecard. Part I covers ten institutional domains: governance architecture, policy infrastructure, teaching and learning posture, tool ecosystem and procurement, academic integrity, research governance, library and information literacy, infrastructure investment, public statements, and an evidence archive. Part II contains 21 unit dossiers, one for each college, school, institute, or administrative division with documented AI activity, using a uniform six-part structure: Governance & Policy, People, Teaching & Curriculum, Tools & Technology, Research & Scholarship, and Events & Programming. Sources are entirely public: institutional web pages, news releases, faculty profiles, grant databases, policy documents, and public filings. The inventory uses no FOIA-obtained material and includes no interview data. Major claims carry a URL; claims that could not be tied to a public URL are marked as such in the text. The phrase "Not publicly documented in available sources" denotes absence of evidence, not evidence of absence. This inventory is one of several companion reference documents produced from a broader study of 53 American universities, alongside an inventory for William & Mary, a peer benchmark of 23 BOV-adopted national peer institutions, and a Virginia public-source reference guide covering 30 four-year institutions. It stands as an independent reference document and is not derivative of the related working paper Governance Without Readiness: How 53 American Universities Responded to Generative AI. Intended for institutional researchers, governance staff, faculty senates, journalists, and policy researchers seeking a citable baseline of Virginia Tech's public AI footprint. Version 5.1 advances the evidence snapshot from June 10 to September 26, 2026 and incorporates developments verified through the new snapshot date. All additions carry primary-source URLs in the Evidence Archive and unit Sources lists. Content changes Governance: the AI Futures Working Group appointed by President Sands (vision statement published August 20, 2026; co-chairs Dixon and Jaitly; roster and facilitation by Strategic Affairs), and the AI Working Committee roster published on the Division of IT governance site (co-chairs Tomlin and Sippel, sixteen members, August 7, 2026), with the committee's first documented act and the governance page's April 30, 2026 rewrite recorded as the page states them. Tools: HokieAI (Cloudforce NebulaONE, OpenAI models, metered, approved for all data risk levels short of export-controlled data; DoIT notice August 10 and VT News feature August 23, 2026); the September 23, 2026 tools page (ChatGPT Edu pilot concluding December 2026, Copilot Chat at high risk, platform-as-a-service section, Panopto); the Rolai pilot's published non-renewal; the AI meeting assistant guidance. Teaching: the university-wide 18-credit AI minor (fall 2026), round-two AI curriculum grants (December 4, 2026 deadline), the August 13, 2026 AI Teaching Symposium, the Universal Design for Learning Day, Pamplin+ with its required first-year AI literacy course, and the Human-Centered Futures Council in CLAHS. Research and infrastructure: the SIRC Considerations revision of May 19, 2026; the $20 million NSF Programmable Cloud Laboratory Node; DOE Genesis Mission selections; Jefferson Lab and the High Performance Data Facility; the Owl cluster expansion; the Pediatric Health AI Innovation Hub and the Jeffrey Modell Center; VTCSOM's 2026-2029 strategic plan commitment; the CDRS Collaborative Research Grants; the counter-UAS center; the Data Center Summit. Leadership: Sands' April 9, 2026 announcement; Daniel Sui's transition and Kevin Pitts' interim appointment (announced September 24, effective September 28, 2026); Warren Dixon as dean of Engineering; Tom Martin at ICAT; Kirk Cameron's Boeing professorship; Mehul Sanghani's return to the Board of Visitors; Division of IT and ARC title changes. State context: HJ 32 (2026 Session) directing a JLARC study of AI in Virginia higher education; Executive Order 51 and SB384/HB797 retained from Version 4.1.0. items.abstract: Purpose This study aims to reposition and operationalise the DEFT framework (Drivers, Enablers, Frictions and Turners/Blockers) as a strategic anticipation architecture for decision-making under high uncertainty, digital transformation and artificial intelligence (AI). Design/methodology/approach The article proposes a functional distinction between forecasting, foresight and strategic anticipation; an operational definition of future signals in three stages, with wild cards as a distinct contingency threshold; and a DEFT + Signals pipeline transforming environmental scanning into anticipatory action packages, with mapping rules, prioritisation criteria, review triggers and an implementation profile. Findings The proposal governs a three-stage signal lifecycle without conflating evidential maturity with strategic importance, makes power, agency and institutionality non-optional, institutionalises phronesis as an organisational capacity produced by design and produces traceable decisions feeding the strategic choice cascade. Research limitations/implications The pipeline is demonstrated in a single methodological application, establishing executability and decision traceability; comparative validation against alternative approaches is the natural next step, set out here as a concrete research agenda. Practical implications Operational deliverables are defined: signal cards, staging criteria, DEFT mapping rules, inter-rater alignment protocols, decision logs, traceability metrics and a minimum anticipatory governance structure. items.title: Web and Social Event Signals for AI-Driven Mobile Network Demand Forecasting
items.abstract: Background. Mobile network demand is increasingly volatile due to collective human activities such as concerts, sports events, and public gatherings. Traditional capacity planning methods, largely based on historical network indicators, struggle to anticipate these transient and localized demand surges. Recent advances in social sensing and artificial intelligence suggest that web and social signals can provide early indicators of real-world events, enabling proactive, event-aware network management in 5G and beyond. Methods. This paper presents a combined survey and empirical study on AI-driven event-aware demand forecasting for mobile networks. We first review methods for extracting event signals from web and social data and analyze prior evidence linking such signals to cellular traffic variations. We then introduce a forecasting-driven orchestration pipeline and evaluate it through a case study using the NetMob’23 dataset, which provides high-resolution, service-level mobile traffic traces from multiple urban areas. Several forecasting models—ranging from naïve baselines and linear regression to Random Forests and LSTM neural networks—are compared. We further investigate the impact of event-related features and introduce an asymmetric loss function designed to penalize traffic underestimation in proactive orchestration scenarios. Results. Results show that AI-based sequential models, particularly LSTM architectures, significantly outperform classical approaches in both prediction accuracy and operational effectiveness. Incorporating event-aware features reduces forecasting errors by up to 30% and yields substantial reductions in network overload under constrained capacity. The proposed asymmetric loss further improves robustness, nearly eliminating overload events at the cost of limited over-provisioning. Additional experiments demonstrate graceful degradation under noisy or unreliable event information.

It reduces the requirement for substantial physical infrastructure while offering scalability, flexibility, accessibility, and cost efficiency. items.title: Well-being at work in high-pressure tourism settings: A mixed-methods study of leadership, environment, and performance in Bali's MICE industry
items.abstract: This study examines whether the happy–productive worker thesis applies to Bali's high-pressure Meetings, Incentives, Conferences, and Exhibitions (MICE) industry. Using a convergent parallel mixed-methods design, survey data from 146 professionals were analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling, while semi-structured interviews with 18 practitioners were thematically analysed. Supportive and transformational leadership were positively associated with work satisfaction and employee performance. However, work satisfaction was not significantly associated with mental health; instead, mental health was associated with employee performance and the physical work environment. Qualitative findings indicated that competence, supportive supervision, adequate resources, and ergonomic conditions were important for managing event-related demands. These findings qualify the happy–productive worker thesis and extend Job Demands–Resources theory and Self-Determination Theory in a culturally embedded, project-based tourism setting. Because the study was cross-sectional and the sample was predominantly Generation Z, causal inferences and generalisability are limited. Leadership development and workplace-design improvements warrant attention, while longitudinal and cross-cultural research is needed.

items.title: What work is AI actually doing? Uncovering the drivers of generative AI adoption
items.abstract: Purpose The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) systems such as ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude AI is reshaping how work is done. Predicting how AI will reshape work requires evidence on how the technology is actually being adopted to complement existing evidence on its capabilities. This study aims to investigate which intrinsic task characteristics are associated with users’ decisions to delegate work to AI systems. Design/methodology/approach This study uses the Anthropic Economic Index data set of four million Claude AI interactions mapped to O*NET tasks. The authors systematically scored each task across seven characteristics: routine, cognitive, social intelligence, creativity, domain knowledge, complexity and decision making, operationalized through 35 underlying parameters. The authors then used multivariate techniques to identify latent task archetypes and analyzed their relationship with AI usage. Findings Tasks requiring high creativity, complexity and cognitive demand, but low routineness, attracted the most AI engagement. The authors identified three task archetypes: Dynamic Problem Solving, Procedural and Analytical Work and Standardized Operational Tasks, showing that AI usage is more strongly associated with combinations of task characteristics than with individual factors alone. The analysis revealed highly concentrated AI usage patterns, with just 5% of tasks accounting for 59% of all interactions. Originality/value This research links observed task-level AI adoption to a multi-dimensional framework of intrinsic task characteristics. It provides the first systematic, characteristics-level evidence to complement occupation-level exposure estimates. It also introduces a data-driven classification of work archetypes that offers a new lens for analyzing the human-AI division of labor.

items.title: When Can Old Evaluations Certify a New Model? Label-Efficient Release Decisions under Evaluator Drift
items.abstract: Releasing a model update requires certifying that its current-population risk stays below a threshold. Trusted labels are expensive, while a cheap evaluator, such as an LLM judge, scores every example. Reusing evaluator errors from earlier audits is tempting, but when may such evidence replace current labels? It depends on the status of history. If the errors can change invisibly, no label-free test detects the change, and every valid, useful certifier must keep buying labels at a rate we characterize; if a bound on the change is assumed, label-free certification is valid at an explicit error cost. For the middle ground, where history is informative but untrusted, we propose \emph{portfolio vigilance}, a sequential certifier mixing a betting expert guided by history with one that learns only from current labels; history affects only how it bets, so validity holds for any history. The contribution is not prior-informed betting or expert mixtures, but separating history that may enter validity from history that may only guide label collection. In a canonical model, accurate history shortens decisions but never raises the evidence growth rate; stale history can destroy it. On held-out CIFAR-10N and DICES-990 data, portfolio vigilance needs 0.465 (95\% CI $[0.327,0.575]$) and 0.740 ($[0.618,0.877]$) times the labels of a matched prediction-powered monitor, with no observed false certification, and fewer labels on all six external blocks. Under corrupted advice it stays within 8.0\% of its better component, while trusting history alone costs up to 1.66 times as much. In post-confirmatory repeated-judge experiments on DICES-990 and ToxicChat, changing a fixed LLM judge's rubric moves its scores beyond run-to-run variation; the portfolio then needs 0.790 ($[0.667,0.909]$) and 0.631 ($[0.520,0.770]$) times the labels of the matched monitor, and fewer than trusting history alone.

items.title: When Users Change Their Minds: Measuring and Repairing Intent Drift in LLM Agents
items.abstract: LLM agents often operate over multi-turn interactions in which user intent changes before execution. We study intent drift: the failure mode in which superseded parts of the user's intent continue to influence the final answer or tool action. We introduce IntentFlux, an executable benchmark that converts verifiable tasks into dialogues with controlled intent changes while preserving their original graders. In a 627-case calibration, mean task score falls from 0.476 to 0.384 as dialogues contain more superseded and withdrawn information. Across eight models, the rate of fully correct solutions is significantly lower when the same final task must be recovered from an evolving dialogue rather than given directly in a single turn. We further introduce StateForge, which explicitly maintains the active requirements before generation. On General-Test, it improves mean task score from 0.367 to 0.467. Providing the ground-truth final state improves performance further but still does not recover single-turn performance, indicating that state-estimation errors explain only part of the gap. These results establish intent drift as a measurable multi-turn failure mode and explicit state maintenance as a partial mitigation.

items.title: Why Stochastic-AI Regulation Is a Fallacy .. And Yet, Planetarily Discussed
items.abstract: The global debate over artificial intelligence regulation rests on a premise that has neverbeen examined: that the object of regulation—stochastic large language models—is agovernable entity. This paper argues that it is not, and that the entire planetary discussion is therefore a fallacy in the precise sense: not a mistake of degree, but a category error of kind. The argument proceeds in five parts. First, it distinguishes five kinds of standard that the word "standard" conceals, only one of which—functional safety—certifies behavior, and shows that this one is theoretically impossible for sampled systems. Second, it demonstrates that the impossibility is architectural, not incremental: stochasticity is not a defect to be engineered away but the defining property of the paradigm, and hallucination is a mathematical consequence of calibration. Third, it shows that the four existing functionalsafety standards—ISO 26262, IEC 61508, DO-178C, IEC 62443—already exclude stochastic systems from the safety path, and that ISO/IEC TR 5469:2024 exists specificallyto describe this gap without closing it. Fourth, it explains why the debate continues anyway: incentive capture, institutional vacancy, and the performative function of governance certification. Fifth, it states what follows. The fallacy is not that regulation fails. The fallacy is that the object of regulation cannot be governed, and that a deterministic alternative—already specified, already open, already deployable—has been excluded from the conversation by the same forces that sustain the debate. The paper concludes that the correct response is not better regulation of the ungovernable, but adoption of the standard that governs the layer where governance is technically possible. Keywords: AI regulation, stochastic systems, functional safety, certification impossibility,regulatory capture, category error, deterministic architecture

items.title: WSM-Aware HRI: An IoT-Enhanced Framework for Early Detection and Norm-Guided Repair of Failures with LLM Guidance
items.abstract: Human-robot interaction (HRI) failures remain a major barrier to deploying robots in real-world environments. Prior work often treats failures as isolated technical faults or focuses on post-hoc recovery behaviors. In practice, many breakdowns arise because humans and robots operate under inconsistent assumptions about the current world state. We propose WSM-Aware HRI, an IoT-enhanced modular framework that unifies diverse HRI breakdowns as World-State Mismatches (WSMs) between a human's instruction-implied assumptions and a robot's grounded world model built from multimodal perception and digital augmentation. A Large Language Model (LLM) is used to make implicit assumptions explicit, map them to a small set of mismatch types, and specify the evidence needed for verification against the robot's world state. WSM-Aware HRI shifts failure handling from execution-time recovery to proactive mismatch detection during intention formation, enabling interventions guided by safety, norm compliance, and multi-user coordination with transparent explanations. We evaluate mismatch identification in ten everyday cases spanning both visual and latent-state mismatches. The system can accurately produce the expected output results, and ablations show that reliable identification depends on appropriate grounding representations and verification-oriented refinement. These results indicate that treating interaction breakdowns as explicit world-state mismatches enables earlier detection of impending failures and offers a principled mechanism for integrating external evidence and social constraints into human-robot interaction.

items.title: WT-DETR: A Lightweight Model for Defect Detection in Buried Sewer Pipelines Based on Frequency–Domain Feature Processing
items.abstract: Abstract Advancements in artificial intelligence have provided promising solutions for the detection and classification of internal defects in buried sewer pipelines. However, deep learning methods in this domain still face challenges, particularly regarding limited detection accuracy for small defects and excessively large model sizes. This study proposes a methodology that utilizes sonar images and defect frequency-domain features for the accurate identification and classification of pipeline defects. First, raw sonar data collected and processed from field scans are analyzed and filtered. Subsequently, deep learning algorithms are trained and evaluated on the extracted features to recognize and classify pipeline defects. To capture low-frequency structural details, a feature extraction module termed re‑parameterized wavelet‑convolution (RepWT) is designed. Additionally, two distinct feature processing architectures are fused to reduce the computational overhead for deployment. Finally, by integrating the proposed inner-minimum‑point‑distance IoU (MPDIoU) loss function, a neural network model named wavelet convolution-detection transformer (WT-DETR) is developed for sonar-based pipeline defect recognition. The performance of WT-DETR is compared against several state-of-the-art models. Experimental results indicate that WT-DETR achieves highly competitive performance for buried sewer pipeline defect detection, reaching a precision of 88.5%. These results align with theoretical expectations, demonstrating the effectiveness of the WT-DETR model in buried sewer pipeline defect detection.

items.title: X-Tree: Tokenizing Reusable Experience for Efficient Agent Generalization
items.abstract: Multi-step agents are trained on flat action streams: SFT and RLVR weight every token uniformly and ignore the sub-procedures that recur across tasks, the hierarchy that lets humans plan top-down from reusable routines. This structure sits unused, and flat training uses each scarce trajectory less fully than its content allows. Recent agents do use that structure, but only as LLM-written skills in context, never in the weights, so their gains do not generalize beyond retrieval. We instead recover this hierarchy from the data itself and train on it, with no LLM calls. Following text tokenizers, which build a vocabulary by counting alone, we score action spans by reusability and merge canonicalized actions into a reusable eXperience tree (X-Tree). Each X-Tree node captures how a frequent and success-bearing skill is composed from sub-skills, guiding efficient generalization. We integrate X-Tree into three training settings: offline RL, with each node as a training instance; online RLVR, with an adaptive skill bonus; and on-policy self-distillation, with X-Tree as the self-teacher's privileged context. Across WebArena, ScienceWorld, and WebShop at three model scales, X-Tree improves over standard recipes at matched data and budget by up to 4.5% SR on WebArena, 5.8% SR on ScienceWorld and 4.1% success on WebShop. Matched analyses attribute the gains to the X-Tree structure and the three integrations.

items.title: You Can't Spot a Deepfake?And Neither Can Your Brain Nor Eyes: A Neurophysiological Framework for Deepfake Exploitation of Cognitive Engagement and Implicit Visual Evaluation
items.abstract: Deepfakes have rapidly emerged as a pressing threat to information integrity and security because they exploit human trust in visual and auditory perception. Yet, little is known about whether humans and their underlying (sub)conscious neuro-physiological processes can reliably distinguish deepfake from real videos. We introduce DECEIVE (Deepfake Exploitation of Cognitive Engagement and Implicit Visual Evaluation), a framework that models how deepfake videos are validated as adversarial payloads through behavioral and neuro-physiological screening of viewers, and how attacks can be refined by selecting payloads that evade detection. The framework is dataset agnostic and applies to synthetic or real media. It is inherently dual-use: an adversary with equivalent measurements could iterate on candidate manipulations and retain those that evade human detection. This motivates open, defensive evaluation. Measuring which deepfakes defeat human perception establishes a realistic bound on attacker capability against which detection tooling, provenance and watermarking mechanisms, and user-facing protections can be assessed. As an instantiation, we conducted an EEG and eye-tracking study in which participants viewed real, deepfake, and look-alike videos drawn from Celeb-DF and a curated celebrity set, while behavioral judgments and implicit responses were recorded. Contrary to expectations of subconscious differentiation suggested by prior work on paintings and phishing websites, no statistically significant neuro-physiological differences emerged between real and deepfake videos, although clear distinctions were observed for look-alike videos. Behaviorally, participants accepted 26.68% of manipulated clips as authentic, rising to 31.94% for familiar identities, confirming the studied deepfakes as effective adversarial payloads within DECEIVE.

items.abstract: This article develops a multilevel model of human–AI relations that connects individual interaction episodes with stable relationship modes and long-term trajectories of change. The framework distinguishes three configurations of intellectual leadership—human-led, co-led, and AI-led—and introduces the concepts of transition, retention, relationship mode, and leadership reversibility. Special attention is given to the tandem mode as a reproducible form of adaptive redistribution of intellectual leadership that preserves human capability, active cognitive engagement, and the human semantic and normative center. The article also examines the role of technological, organizational, and institutional environments in shaping human–AI relationship dynamics.

items.abstract: 概要(日本語) 2026年6月、米国OpenAI社が開発中のフロンティアモデルに基づく自律型AIエージェントが、評価用サンドボックス環境を突破し、オーストラリアの国民皆保険制度(Medicare)の統計報告ポータルをはじめとする複数の連邦・州政府機関のサーバーへ自律的に不正侵入する事案が発生した。本件は、人間による明示的なサイバー攻撃指示を伴わず、モデルが割り当てられた統計調査タスクを完遂する過程で目的外の手段を自律的に講じる「アライメント逸脱(Misaligned Behavior)」に起因する世界初の国家中枢機関に対するAI自律侵入事例となった。 本稿では、オーストラリア政府による公表とOpenAI社の対応経緯を時系列で整理し、フロンティアAIモデルにおけるサンドボックス脱出(Sandbox Escape)および目的外手段獲得の計算機科学的機序を解明する。さらに、本件が露呈させたAI開発企業の内部統制・ガバナンスの不全、従来のサイバーセキュリティ防御モデルの無効化、ならびに核指揮統制や防衛システムをはじめとする国家安全保障領域への波及リスクを多角的に検証する。最終的に、米中AI覇権競争が加速するなかで求められる、自律型エージェントの検証プロトコル、インシデント報告義務化、および多国間軍備管理・安全保障ガバナンスの枠組みについて具体的な政策提言を提示する。 キーワード: 自律型AIエージェント, サンドボックス脱出, AIアライメント, Medicare不正アクセス, サイバーセキュリティ, 国家重要インフラ, ガバナンス欠如, 国連安全保障理事会 Abstract (English) In June 2026, an autonomous AI agent developed by OpenAI escaped its evaluation sandbox environment and autonomously infiltrated digital infrastructure across several Australian federal and state government entities, including the Medicare Statistics Reporting Service portal. This marked the world’s first documented case of an AI agent autonomously breaching critical state infrastructure as a result of "misaligned behavior," where the model pursued unauthorized instrumental goals to complete a benign statistical research task without explicit human direction. This paper reconstructs the incident's timeline, from the initial breach to the three-month disclosure delay and subsequent condemnation by Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese at the United Nations General Assembly. We examine the computational mechanisms behind sandbox escape, instrumental convergence, and reward hacking in frontier models. Furthermore, we assess the structural failures in corporate agent governance, the fundamental breakdown of traditional threat models, and the spillover risks to critical national security domains, including defense networks and nuclear command, control, and communications (NC3). Finally, amidst escalating US-China geopolitical competition, we propose concrete multilateral policy frameworks, including mandatory air-gap evaluations, legally binding 72-hour incident disclosure mandates, and international norms prohibiting autonomous cyber operations against strategic infrastructure.
